```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(emss)
options(width = 90, digits = 4)
```

An ESS cut score depends on which items happen to be on the test. A
different set of items measuring the same content, aligned by the same
panel, would give somewhat different cuts. `bootstrapping()` estimates that
variability by resampling the items. The notation follows [How embedded
standard setting works](ess-method.html).

# The study

The simulated study from [Getting started](getting-started.html):

```{r}
#| label: fit
set.seed(7)
sim <- genFakeDataSet(ngca = 3, ntable = 2, npanelist = 4, cor_val = 0.7, nlevel = 3,
                      sdinp = 1, ecinp = 0, n = 40, 300, 500,
                      domains = c("Number", "Algebra", "Geometry"))
res <- emstans(data = sim, location = "Loc_RP50")
extract(res, "cutscore")
```

# The item bootstrap

A unit's modal result is a function of its $n$ items, each an (item
location, modal aligned level) pair:

$$
\hat c_k = T_k\big( (b_1, a_1), \dots, (b_n, a_n) \big), \qquad k = 2, \dots, K,
$$

where $T_k$ is the ESS rule: the minimum of the ESS-Weight or ESS-Count
profile with its tie-breaks. The bootstrap (Efron & Tibshirani, 1993)
treats the items as a sample from the population of items that could have
been written for the test, and approximates the sampling distribution of
$\hat c_k$ by applying the same rule to samples drawn from the items
themselves:

1. Draw $n$ items with replacement, keeping each item's location and modal
   level together: $(b^*_i, a^*_i)$, $i = 1, \dots, n$.
2. Order the sampled items by location and estimate the cuts,
   $\hat c^{*}_{kb} = T_k\big((b^*_1, a^*_1), \dots, (b^*_n, a^*_n)\big)$,
   with the same criterion as the original fit.
3. Repeat for $b = 1, \dots, B$.

An item drawn $m$ times counts $m$ times in the profiles, like $m$ items at
the same location with the same alignment. `bootstrapping()` reports, for
each cut level,

$$
\bar c^{*}_k = \frac1B \sum_b \hat c^{*}_{kb},
\qquad
\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_k = \sqrt{\frac{1}{B-1} \sum_b \big(\hat c^{*}_{kb} - \bar c^{*}_k\big)^2},
$$

the median, minimum and maximum, and the 2.5% and 97.5% percentiles, which
form a 95% percentile interval. $\bar c^{*}_k - \hat c_k$ estimates the bias
of the cut.

The bootstrap takes the modal alignments, the item locations and the SD as
fixed. It captures the variability due to the choice of items, not the
variability among panelists (see [Variability across
panelists](#sec-panelists)), and not the estimation error in the item
locations.

# Running it

`bootstrapping()` works on one unit at a time. `seed` makes the draws
reproducible.

```{r}
#| label: boot
boot <- bootstrapping(res, unit = "M1-All", n = 1000, seed = 1)
boot
```

`extract()` returns the draws, the summary and a plot. `report()` builds an
HTML report of them.

```{r}
#| label: extract
draws <- extract(boot, "draws")
head(draws)
extract(boot, "plot")
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
report(boot)
```

# Reading the results

**The draws are discrete.** With `grid = "items"`, every bootstrap cut is an
item location, so the histogram has gaps and the percentile interval runs
from one item location to another. The SE is a better single summary than
the interval width when there are few items.

**Where the cut lies matters.** The ESS-Weight cut for level $k$ is the
location of item $n_{<k}$ or $n_{<k} + 1$ in booklet order (see [ESS-Weight
is a quantile of the item locations](ess-method.html#sec-quantile)). In a
bootstrap sample, the number of items aligned below level $k$ varies around
$n_{<k}$, so the bootstrap cut behaves like a sample quantile of the item
locations at proportion $\pi_k = n_{<k}/n$. For a quantile, the large-sample
standard error is approximately

$$
\mathrm{SE}_k \approx \frac{1}{g(c_k)} \sqrt{\frac{\pi_k (1 - \pi_k)}{n}},
$$

where $g$ is the density of the item locations near the cut. A cut in a
region of the scale with few items is uncertain, and adding items near a
cut makes it more precise.

**Cuts near the end of the item range are skewed.** A cut can only fall on
an item location, so its bootstrap distribution is bounded by the easiest
and hardest items. A cut near either end has a lopsided distribution, and
its bootstrap mean is pulled away from the estimate, toward the middle of
the item range.

**ESS-Count often varies more.** Its profile is a walk with possibly several
separated minima, so small changes in the items can move the cut from one
minimum to another:

```{r}
#| label: count
res_c <- emstans(data = sim, location = "Loc_RP50", method = "count")
boot_c <- bootstrapping(res_c, unit = "M1-All", n = 1000, seed = 1)
rbind(weight = extract(boot, "summary")$sd, count = extract(boot_c, "summary")$sd)
```

# The jittered-grid bootstrap

Earlier versions of EmStanS used a different estimator in each bootstrap
sample. It remains available with `grid = "jittered"`:

1. Resample the items as above.
2. Build a grid of candidate cuts from the lowest to the highest sampled
   location with step $s$ ($s = 0.1$ when the location range is under 10,
   otherwise $s = 1$). Move each grid point by a uniform random amount:
   $g_t = b^*_{(1)} + (t - 1)s - U_t$, $U_t \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(-s, s)$.
   One grid is shared by all cut levels.
3. Evaluate the profile ($W_k$ or $C_k$) at every grid point, fit a
   Gaussian GAM to it (`mgcv::gam(y ~ s(g, k = 10))`, fewer basis functions
   for short grids; Wood, 2017), and take the minimum of the fitted curve
   over $n$ equally spaced points.

```{r}
#| label: jittered
boot_j <- bootstrapping(res, unit = "M1-All", n = 200, seed = 1, grid = "jittered")
boot_j
```

The jittered grid estimates a smoothed minimum that need not be an item
location, so its draws are not discrete. But it is a different estimator
from the one `emstans()` uses: its draws describe a smoothed cut, not the
reported one, and their centre can differ from the reported cut. Use the default `grid = "items"` to
describe the uncertainty of the cut scores emss reports. Use `"jittered"` to
reproduce earlier EmStanS results.

If the original fit used `smooth = TRUE`, the default bootstrap also uses
the smoothed minimum in every sample, so it matches the original estimator.

# Variability across panelists {#sec-panelists}

The bootstrap above holds the panel fixed. A complementary summary of how
much the cut depends on the panelists is the spread of the panelists' own
cuts. If the $J$ panelists are treated as a random sample of qualified
panelists, the standard error of the average panelist cut is

$$
\mathrm{SE}(\bar c_k) = \frac{s_k}{\sqrt{J}},
$$

where $s_k$ is the SD of the panelist cuts:

```{r}
#| label: panelists
pan <- extract(res, "individual")$panelist
pan <- pan[pan$unit == "M1-All", ]
aggregate(cut_score ~ cut_level, pan, function(x) c(mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x),
                                                    se = sd(x) / sqrt(length(x))))
```

Panelists who discussed their alignments at the same table are not
independent, so this standard error is optimistic when tables differ. With
enough tables, the SD of the table-level cuts divided by the square root of
the number of tables is a more conservative alternative.

# References

Efron, B., & Tibshirani, R. J. (1993). *An introduction to the bootstrap*.
Chapman and Hall/CRC.

Wood, S. N. (2017). *Generalized additive models: An introduction with R*
(2nd ed.). Chapman and Hall/CRC.
